A Brief History of Civil Rights in Lamandica:

Civil rights are an integral aspect of everyday Lamandican society. Lamandicans hold this right in high regard and are often thankful to be living in one of the freest nations in Elseyr.
The value of expansive civil rights for Lamandicans directly is a result of Lamandicas predecessor, the Columbian Union. In the Columbian Union, civil liberties were nonexistent. Those who would speak out against the oppressive regimes of the early 1700s were either imprisoned or executed. Lamandicans didnt have a say government, as there were either no elections, and the few that did occur were rigged. Very few Lamandicans were allowed to own land. Minorities in Lamandica were treated with the most hostility. This is most evident with the 1715 Ounthrouppsville Massacre, when government officials executed innocent civilians in a minority neighborhood of Tenahaston.
All these injustices for the Lamandican people led up to the War of Lamandican Independence (17211727), where many Lamandicans rebelled against the government, including Charles Deverine I, Daniel Barton Foster, and James Marckogann, causing the last of the oppressive regimes of the Columbian Union to be overthrown in 1726.
With victory imminent for the rebels, many high-ranking Lamandican officials met in Taultion to discuss the founding principles of the new nation of Lamandica. What is now referred to as the Manaubs Convention, led by Charles Deverine I and James Marckogann, focused mainly on what rights the people should have in this new nation. Seeing as the citizens of the Columbian Union were heavily regulated, censored, and suppressed, the founding fathers of Lamandica envisioned a nation where citizens could say whatever they felt without being prosecuted, and express themselves without fear of any consequences. These principles established at the Manaubs Convention helped shape the nation of Lamandica today as a free, inclusive nation.

Sender: [i]President Fereydun Khan of Dhornaper[/i]
To: [i]Minister of Industry Jarl Holmgeir IV. of Reikyawik[/i]

Thank you Minister for your kind words and speedy response.

I am thankful for your explanation of the conflict. I find the situation worrisome and remain rather confused how events between two nations, which could have been settled diplomatically, have escalated to such an extraordinary scale. Dhornaper is, of course, neutral and will not be involved in the conflict. Our current understanding of the situation is very poor.

Regarding trade, Dhornaper has ample natural resources in aluminum, oil, and iron which we are willing to exchange for coal required for our manufacturing industries. We are willing to exchange these or pay money in fair amounts for 20 million tons of coal per year.
